speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table
order in council P.C. 2474, dated June 24, 1947, proclaiming section 14 of the National Housing Act. Witlh the permission of the house I should like to make a brief statement by way of explanation. Section 14 of the National Housing Act provides for loans to assist in the construction of houses on farms.
When speaking in the house on July 29 last on the amendments to the National Housing Act, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply stated that the farm-lending section of the act would be brought into force by proclamation. He explained that much preparatory work had to be done in developing a suitable procedure for making farm loams. Negotiations had to be conducted with the lending institutions. Mortgage forms had to be prepared for each province. In their preparation it was intended -that new ground would be broken in respect of grain-growing farms in the prairie provinces. The old form of mortgage with the crop share lease did not meet the circumstances of farmers in the grain-growing areas. A new method of mortgage repayment was required which would provide an adequate escape clause for distress years and payments in good crop years which increase in direct proportion to the yield and value of the crop.
Before the new form of mortgage could be applied, certain adjustments in provincial legislation in each of the prairie provinces were considered necessary. Accordingly, discussions were held early in the year with the governments of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, when the proposed mortgage form and repayment formula were reviewed. Subsequent to these meetings, written submissions were made to each province detailing what legislative changes were required.
The necessary amending legislation was not passed by any of the prairie legislatures at this year's sessions. There was, however, a good

Questions
deal of interest shown in the proposals, and negotiations are being continued with the governments concerned.
In the meantime, however, the facilities of section 14 will be available to farmers in six of the provinces. So far as the prairie provinces are concerned-, it is not intended that loans will be made on grain-growing farms until satisfactory arrangements have been completed for using a flexible payment mortgage. The ordinary payment mortgage on this type of farm does not meet the circumstances of farmers whose incomes fluctuate widely from year to year, owing to variations in grain yields and value. Applications, however, will be considered from farmers in Manitoba and Alberta who do not operate farms which are primarily grain growing in character, and where Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation considers the orthodox money payment mortgage to be satisfactory. The facilities of the act will not be extended to any kind of farm in Saskatchewan until more general farm debt legislation problems are clarified.
An explanatory booklet entitled "Farm Housing Loans" is being prepared by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This will be sent to farmers in reply to inquiries about the facilities of the National Housing Act. The booklet explains the provisions of section 14 and outlines the procedure by which farmers make application for loans. Farmers are asked to direct inquiries to the nearest regional or branch office of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.

speechtext:
1.	Are retired bankers, who paid income taxes to the government on their total salaries from 1924 to 1946 and possibly from 1918 to 1924, exempt from paying income taxes today on that portion contributed by them for superannuation during this period?
2.	If so, for what reason?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
subtopic: INCOME TAX-SUPERANNUATION
speechtext:
1.	Yes, but only on such portion of their pension as is attributable to contributions made by them during the years 1928 to 1945 inclusive.
2. Subsection 1 (h) of section 5 of the Income War Tax Act as enacted by 18-19 George V, chapter 12 (1928) provided that where the trustees or administrators of any employees' superannuation or pension fund elected thereunder to have the investment income of such fund exempt from taxation, the employees' contributions thereto would not be allowed as a deduction in determining their taxable income. Moreover, in such event, the pension ultimately payable to the employee was made exempt from tax only to such proportion of the total amount paid by him into the fund as was so paid after the effective date of the said election.
The trustees of all bank pension funds elected to have the investment income thereof exempt from tax and as a result all bank pensions now being paid are tax free to the extent provided by such formula.

This formula is, of course, also applicable to all other pensions paid from funds in respect of which the trustees similarly elected.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ITALY, ROUMANIA, HUNGARY AND FINLAND- APPROVAL OF TREATIES SIGNED AT PARIS, FEBRUARY 10, 1947
speechtext:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the treaties of peace with Italy, 'Roumania, Hungary and Finland, signed at Paris on the 10th February, 4947, and that this house do approve the same.
He said: Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that a conference for the conclusion of peace treaties with Italy, Roumania, Bulgaria, Hungary and Finland was held in Paris from July 29 to October 15, 1946. The delegates from Canada were my hon. colleague, the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and myself. As Prime Minister and, at the time, Secretary of State for External Affairs, I was chairman of the Canadian delegation. As I was not able to be in Paris throughout the entire meeting of the conference, my colleague later on became chairman of the Canadian delegation. The alternates were: N. A. Robertson, then Undersecretary of State for External Affairs; A. D. P. Heeney, Clerk of the Privy Council; Major General G. P. Vanier, DS.O., M.C., Canadian Ambassador to France; L. D. Wilgress, then Canadian Ambassador to the U.S.S.R.; Lieutenant General Maurice Pope, C.B., M.C., head of the Canadian military mission to the allied control commission, Germany.	The
advisers were C. S. A. Ritchie and J. A. Qhapdelaine, of the Department of External Affairs, and J. A. Gibson, of the Prime Minister's office. Mr. S. F. Rae acted as secretary of the delegation.
On February 10 last the Canadian Ambassador to France, Major General Vanier, on behalf of the Canadian government, signed, in Paris, peace treaties with Italy, Roumania, Hungary and Finland. On the same day the Secretary of State for External Affairs made a statement on the work of the Paris conference, and tabled the texts of the treaties in this house. The statement was supplemented by a report on the proceedings of the conference, prepared by the Minister of National Defence. The report was printed as an annex
Treaties oj Peace

to the Votes and Proceedings of that date. Copies of the peace treaties were subsequently distributed to all members of parliament.
The main purpose of these treaties is to bring to an end formally the state of war existing between Italy, Roumania, Hungary and Finland on the one hand, and the allied and associated powers on the other. The settlements will dispose of many important issues of a political, economic or military character outstanding between the governments of these enemy states and the allies as a result of the war. The formal termination of the state of war which exists between ourselves and the enemy countries is a necessary step in the reestablishment of a peaceful world.
Canada, one of the twenty-one nations invited to participate in .the Paris conference, was given an opportunity to examine and comment on the draft treaties as prepared in the council of foreign ministers. The Canadian delegation played a part in drawing up the conference recommendations which were used to a considerable extent by the council of foreign ministers in preparing the treaties in final form. While an earlier and more effective association of Canada and certain other allies might have resulted in an improvement of these settlements, it is probably fair to say that in the circumstances the treaties represent the best resolution possible of the conflicting interests amongst the major allies.
The entry into force of these treaties is a necessary first stage in the reconstruction of the economic life of Europe. In many cases the restrictions operative in the enemy states under the armistice terms make long-range planning by the governments of these countries difficult. Until the peace treaties are implemented the uncertainties inherent in the armistice regimes will continue.
One of the results of the entry into effect of the treaties will be the withdrawal of occupation forces from the ex-enemy satellite states, subject to the right of the Soviet union to keep sufficient forces in Roumania and Hungary to maintain lines of communication with its occupation zone in Austria.
It is provided in the preambles to these treaties that their conclusion will enable the allied and associated powers to support the application of each of the enemy states concerned for membership in the united nations. If these states eventually become members of the united nations they will be able to participate in common action on international problems through the united nations. Eventual applications for membership from these states
JMr. Mackenzie King.]
will, of course, be judged by the Canadian government on their merits and in the light of existing circumstances.
Because of the advantages which would derive from a termination of the state of war with these states, it appears desirable that parliamentary approval should be given to the treaties at this time.
The approval by the two houses of parliament of the treaties does not imply their immediate ratification by Canada. To this end, two steps must thereafter be taken. First, a submission must be made with the approval of the governor in council to the king, asking for the execution by his majesty of instruments of ratification. Second, the instruments of ratification signed by the king must be deposited as provided for in the treaties.
The final articles of each of the treaties provide that the entry into force of the treaties will depend in the first instance upon the deposit of instruments of ratification by certain of the great powers which are members of the council of foreign ministers. In the case of Italy, these are the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, the United Kingdom, the United States of America, and France. In the case of Hungary and Roumania the deposit of instruments of ratification by the Soviet union, the United Kingdom, and the United States of America is required. The treaty of peace with Finland will come into force when the Soviet, union and United Kingdom have deposited their instruments of ratification. The treaties of peace will not, how'ever, enter into force as far as Canada and the other allied' or associated powers are concerned until their separate instruments of ratification have been deposited.
Although the governments of the United Kingdom, the United States of America and France have now obtained approval, through their respective legislative processes, for the ratification of the various treaties, none of the great powers has as yet taken the final step of depositing its instruments of ratification.
Hon. members will have seen that on June 5 the United States senate approved the Italian treaty by a vote of 79 to 10, and the treaties with Roumania, Bulgaria and Hungary by an unrecorded voice vote.
The texts of the peace treaties make it clear that Canada could not terminate the state of war existing between this country and the respective enemy states by depositing the Canadian instruments of ratification prior to the treaties having been brought into force by the responsible great powers.

Treaties oj Peace
Accordingly, while the government is seeking parliamentary approval for the treaties at this time, it is not anticipated that Canada's instruments of ratification will be deposited' until the great powers, whose ratification is necessary before the treaties can come into effect, have deposited their instruments of ratification.

subtopic: ITALY, ROUMANIA, HUNGARY AND FINLAND- APPROVAL OF TREATIES SIGNED AT PARIS, FEBRUARY 10, 1947
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to make a few observations with regard to the four treaties of peace now before us for approval, first I desire to say to you and to the house that these matters do throw into relief the whole question of our foreign relations as they may affect the continent of Europe and the peace of the world in general. Since the signing of these four treaties of peace on February 10, 1947-and perhaps this might be said with even greater force of the fact that the conference and the discussions generally commenced almost a year ago-much water has gone under the international bridge; and perhaps a brief review of the situation would not be out of place to indicate our present position in relation to the treaties themselves.
While the question of the making of treaties of peace is of great importance as between vanquished and victor, I think it can be said properly and with emphasis that the problem which faced the nations of the world at the Paris conference was not just that of finding some method of reaching agreement between victor and vanquished but rather one of reaching agreement between victor and victor. These considerations bring out more prominently the problem of the competing ideologies which are so prevalent today, and which have focused world attention upon Europe, and particularly upon central and southeastern Europe. Since the meeting of the council of foreign ministers which preceded the Paris conference, and since that conference itself, while the picture perhaps has not changed so much, the developments arising out of the situation there have moved into clearer perspective so far as we in Canada are concerned. I do not think there is much use trying to gloss over with fancy words the issues that lie at the root of the problem of making peace in Europe. I believe most of us realize that the world has moved forward from the idealism, shall I say, which seemed to grip the nations at the first great security conference at San Francisco to a more realistic appreciation of the situation, so that today the blunt phraseology and direct approach on the part of the big powers toward each other show very clearly the issues involved in Europe, upon which these treaties now direct 83166-308
the attention of this country. I believe it would be remiss on the part of Canadians generally, and particularly on the part of this parliament, if we did not take some notice of the situation which exists there.
In the case of the Italian treaty we have a situation which is of major concern to the people of Canada. Here we had a compromise settlement with respect to the great problem of Trieste, a settlement which the Secretary of State of the United States was pleased to report upon to his President and to the American people, in the early days of the conference, in this way:
The greatest struggle was over the Italian treaty, and the greatest issue involved in that treaty was the fate of Trieste and adjacent territory along the western shore of the Istrian peninsula. The American delegation, supported by the French and British, urged that Trieste and adjacent territory which are predominantly Italian, should remain with Italy, and the predominantly Slavic hinterland should go to Yugoslavia.
The position in which every nation now finds itself, so far as approval of the treaty of peace with Italy is concerned, is one attended by a feeling of danger. There is some question whether the present set-up for Italy, as outlined at the Paris conference and for which approval is asked of parliament today, does not leave the Italian people in a defenceless position in the face of what might be known as rigorous ideological aggression in that part of Europe.
We in Canada believe that the democratic way of life is the way which, with due regard to freedom and liberty, we should encourage other nations of the world to follow. Certainly it is the desire of this country and of the Canadian people that the people of Italy should be encouraged in every possible way to see that democracy as we understand it shall have a chance to take root in that country, to grow and to develop, so that under a democratic system of government Italy, as was envisaged this afternoon by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), may once more take its place as a peace-loving nation within the framework of the united nations organization.
The difficulty in the compromise treaty with Italy-and it is a difficulty of which I believe the people of Canada ought to be made aware -is that while to a great extent, and quite properly, Italy has been stripped of her warmaking potentials, nevertheless by virtue of this treaty of peace we have left her almost unarmed and unprotected. We have taken away from her the port of Trieste-and I am not specifically objecting to that at this moment, having in mind the necessity for

Treaties oj Peace

compromise. Alongside her we have left what statistics would seem to indicate as a standing Yugoslavian army numbering somewhere around 500,000 men. The danger is further aggravated by the fact that some $360 million is to come from the people of Italy in the payment of reparations. A large part of that money will go to Yugoslavia, to Soviet Russia and to the satellite states which seem to have such a close alignment with marxian policies.
Those of us in the House of Commons who are interested in external affairs would be remiss in our duty were we not to point out to the house and to the people generally the dangers inherent in the settlement of the Italian peace. I take personal encouragement from the Prime Minister's remarks of a few moments ago, which I believe were to some extent a repetition of what was said a few days ago in the house by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent). Both right hon. gentlemen have stated that these treaties will not necessarily mean that Canada will rush in with great haste in an attempt to put its imprimatur upon what may readily be regarded as a matter of grave consequence to the peace of Europe and the welfare of our own people in general.
I am not taking that position of opposing the approval of these treaties. I do not see how we can very well avoid giving approval, because Canada's word has already been given. Having in mind, however the fact that so many changes have taken place in the meantime, there seems to be some additional argument as to why we should not have moved more quickly than we did. Certainly we should not have moved more quickly than we have moved in trying to put any part of Europe in either a political, economic or financial straitjacket. Those of us who have had the opportunity, even in a minor capacity, of seeing the economic disaster and the financial and physical destruction in certain countries of Europe must realize that many years will have passed before those people will have the opportunity, from the standpoint of their economy, actually to get back on their feet. Anyone who remembers the great piles of rubble, the vast devastation, almost unbelievable, unless one sees it, will realize the truth of what I am saying. One must contrast the physical and other conditions of Europe with our own difficulties. We realize that, great as are our own problems in connection with reconstruction and building, in Europe today they have not even begun in many places to clear up the rubble, let alone to lay foundations, let alone to finish building, let alone to begin again to do business. That, in simple language, is
[Mx. Graydon.]
just about the position in which Europe is placed today. As to a peace settlement in Europe I have always felt that we must be most careful not too soon to put any part of Europe into either an economic or a political straitjacket. Europe is in a much different position from any other part of the world. We have seen the changes which have taken place since the Paris peace conference, and we can visualize changes which may develop to affect the views of many people who were at that conference. Having these points in mind I say we ought to go slowly and carefully in giving approval to matters of this kind.
While I am not sure that I subscribe to it, there is a school of thought which holds that the four peace treaties-actually there were five, but we consider only the four, owing to the fact that from the technical point of view Bulgaria was not at war with us-and the whole quesiton of Europe's rehabilitation and reconstruction, economically and politically, ought to have been dealt with as one major problem. It is felt by some that we should have said to Russia: You have certain problems and certain designs; you have certain policies you think should be applied in Europe; let us see what you want in Europe, and we will place beside it what we think is necessary there. It is considered that those major issues should have been the subject of one decision; that we ought not to have grappled only with the comparatively easy tasks related to the smaller nations such as Hungary and Finland, but that we should have dealt with the whole broad picture, including Germany, Austria and the other nations. In other words it is considered that an attempt should have been made to deal with the whole problem of Europe as on one political, economic and financial basis.
As I have said, that is the view put forward by some practical men who have studied the position in Europe. I am not sure that I subscribe to it. It is possible that after careful consideration the big five powers decided it was best to deal first *with these minor matters, in the hope that by dealing with matters which would cause the least friction and division they might reach a formula with the aid of which they could deal with the larger problems ahead.
While this whole question has arisen with respect to the problem in Europe, we are now asked in parliament to deal with Hungary. Those of us who have watched the developments in Hungary in recent times will realize the changed situation or at least the major developments which have occurred in that

Treaties oj Peace
strife-torn country of eastern Europe. There is a changed government there which has led to suspicion on the part of the western powers, particularly one of the great western democracies which has protested vehemently and violently as to the motives and sources underlying the powers which seem to have called for that change of government. The Hungary of February 10, 1947, is in many respects a different Hungary from the Hungary of the present day in connection with which we are asked to approve this treaty. This only bears out some of the arguments which have been brought forward by people in other parts of the world and which I think are at least worthy of consideration by this house.
I am not going to deal at length with these matters because after all they should have been dealt with at an earlier stage when we could have discussed the whole question of our foreign relations in Europe. When Canada went to the peace conference a good many people thought that we were going on an equal footing with the other nations attending that conference. As I understand it, Canada actually was never asked to make a decision with respect to these peace treaties at the Paris conference. Under the procedure which was set up and which was subsequently followed, she was permitted to make recommendations along with a great number of other countries. But those recommendations were limited as to extent and as to the grounds upon which they were made. They were further limited, may I say, by there being no guarantee whatsoever that the council of foreign ministers would do more than consider the recommendations which had been made by Canada or which had been agreed to by the powers in general. In a sense we were acting only as a sort of general adviser with respect to the thing without being even in the position of real advisers.

Having in mind the fact that the press from all over the world was represented generously at the conference, journalists of twenty-seven countries took an official poll of the Paris peace conference when it had come to an end. Three questions were asked in the poll: First, did the press men regard the conference as a success; second, did they regard it as a failure, or, third, did they regard it as a farce. Of those journalists, thirty-one replied that they considered it had been a success; 56 stated that it had been a failure, and 33 said that they believed it had been a farce. The proportion of criticism as against approval was therefore more than two to one. The great Winston Churchill, commenting upon the conference, said that he regarded it as bad diplomacy but perhaps it could be considered as valuable education for the future.
Apparently Canada has found that there was some good education in it as well as a number of good lessons to be gained. After we had gone through the experience of the Paris conference, where our voice was just about an international whisper, as far as I can gather-there was not much more allowed to us than that-we took a stand in connection with the Moscow conference which dealt with the German and Austrian treaties. I was one, and I think the house was almost a unit in taking this view, who supported Canada's position with respect to greater and fuller participation in that great conference at Moscow. We did not get very far with our proposals and suggestions, but on the other hand those who were at Moscow did not seem to get very far either in the development, of the business which lay "at their door at that time- As I said in a previous debate- I want to repeat it now because of its relevancy to the subject-it seems to me that Canada ought to have raised a greater and more powerful voice at Paris instead of waiting until afterward to raise the voice that was finally raised in January of this year. Having had the embarrassing experience, along with some other nations, of not being granted an equal voice in connection with the treaty making in Paris, I think we ought to have taken a stand which would have been more effective and would have carried more weight than anything done at a later time.
So fas as Canada's part in the peace conference at Paris was concerned, our policy, as was stated by the Prime Minister in one of his addresses, was to assist in the revival of European political democracy. With that statement I think Canadians generally will

be in agreement. I am not so sure that we followed the line that this country ought to have followed in connection with the Paris conference. I say that with some diffidence, because it seems to me that we departed and retreated so far as the Paris conference was concerned from our multiple party system of delegations in external affairs matters. It might be that that case was not on all fours with some of the meetings to which this country has been invited from time to time, but it did have the effect of the government being the only ones in full possession of the facts relating to the whole problem of the peace treaties and to what went on over there. Everything is not always on record in connection with international conferences. There are questions of background, there are the other vital problems which face the delegates from time to time. These are important factors in any international conclave. As the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence were the only members of the house who were there, I think the government might well have seen to it that these treaties were referred to the standing committee on external affairs so that detailed consideration might have been given to their provisions. I do not believe we are taking the proper stand in connection with these matters (by simply having a resolution brought before the house concerning treaties as to the background of which the government itself is the only one who has any inside knowledge. As I understand it, a resolution such as this goes through only one stage. It does not provide opportunity for examination of the Prime Minister or the Minister of National Defence, who were there. It leaves this and other parties on this side of the house in the position of having to take it or leave it.
I suggest to the Prime Minister and to the Secretary of State for External Affairs in view of the problems which this matter raises in connection with our foreign relations, if there ever was a time when the standing committee on external affairs ought to be given an opportunity of doing a first class and comprehensive job it is on peace treaties. It is not only a matter of the technical approval of these treaties. This house has never had enough debating opportunities on the whole problem of Canada's policy on foreign relations. In this parliament we cannot hope to keep abreast of the obligations we are assuming in the international field.
As the Prime Minister indicated in one of his earlier addresses this session, we were at seventeen world conferences in 1939, and
[Mr. Graydou.l
Canada was officially represented at ninety-eight last year. If one looks over the whole field of our development of external affairs he will see that it is hopelessly out of joint, shall I say, when compared with the length of time that is provided and the opportunities given parliament for a full and comprehensive discussion of our foreign policy. It is not enough, as I say, in this particular case, simply to refer to this as a technical matter of the approval of treaties. This brings into the spotlight the whole problem of our foreign relations in Europe. If there is anything more important to parliament and to the Canadian people than our foreign relations in Europe, I should like to know what it is; because the whole question of peace or war, and the security of our homes and of our people, are hound up in seeing to it that the peace of Europe is firmly and properly established. When these peace treaties come back from the external affairs committee, where I hope the government will send them, this house should have an opportunity, on a motion for concurrence in the report, to have a full, detailed and lengthy debate, even at this stage of the session, because after all, time can be taken off some other less important things. The house is entitled to know the government's policy and to, have it fully discussed and laid bare to the people of Canada. I do not think this house should prorogue until such time as the foreign relations of Canada are fully and properly debated on the floor of the house.

Not that the committee could change them, any more than this house can; but we could get some information in regard to them and understand their implications better and the conditions with which we are confronted in Europe, so that we could decide whaJt we should do. The ratification of these treaties by parliament will, I understand, bring to an end hostilities between ourselves and the European countries concerned, and we must all welcome that. For some time I have been firmly of the opinion that the war will not be ended for us, nor will the danger of another war be over, until we have rehabilitated the countries that were devastated economically by war, so that they can again take their normal place in word affairs. Hon. members who have been privileged to visit Europe in the last few years knows of the devastation that has taken place in these countries. It was not only destruction of material things. It was more than that; it was an upheaval

Treaties oj Peace
that destroyed their normal way of life, and that is perhaps more difficult to restore than their economic stability. Therefore I hope that this government and this parliament will do everything possible in an economic way to assist the countries of Europe to regain their feet. Any expense we may incur in doing that should be considered as a war expense, because until these countries are economically reestablished, peace is never safe.
I suppose the treaties represent the best that could be done under the circumstances in which the peace conference was held, with all the differences, ideological and others, between parties who were at one time allies and had taken part in framing these treaties.

I doubt whether it is not too late in this session for that to be done this year, but I hope the government will take note of it and that they will not let an opportunity of this kind pass another time.

speechtext:
As the member of the delegation who following the departure of the Prime Minister on August 25, 1946, until October 15, 1946, had the honour of leading the Canadian delegation in Paris, it would perhaps be proper if I said a few words before the motion is put. It is thoroughly understood that the purpose of the conference was not to draft treaties of peace.
Canada declared war on Italy on June 10, 1940, and on Roumania, Hungary and Finland
Treaties of Peace

on December 7, 1941, in consequence of states of war having been brought about by those countries. The purpose of this resolution is to authorize approval of the treaties of peace which have been prepared to end the state of war which existed between the twenty-one allied governments and four of the satellites of Germany. The treaties represent the work of the council of foreign ministers at the Paris conference over a period of some eighteen months. These treaties, as finally drafted by the council of foreign ministers, were put before the house on February 10, when the Secretary of State for External Affairs made a brief statement. At that time the report by myself on the work of the Canadian delegation at the Paris conference was tabled and printed as an appendix to Votes and Proceedings. The treaties of peace have therefore been before this house and the Canadian people for some four months, and that has given an ample opportunity to hon. members and others to examine the treaties and see what they contain.
The Paris conference itself stemmed from the Potsdam conference which was held in July 1944. At that conference the heads of the governments of the United Kingdom, the United States and the U.S.S.R. issued a protocol on August 2, 1945 providing for the establishment of a council of foreign ministers composed of representatives of their three governments, as well as of France and China. The council was charged with the task of drawing up treaties of peace with five of the .satellites of Germany in order that these draft treaties might be submitted to the members of the united nations who had taken a substantial part in the war against these five countries. This work of preparation was to be done by the representatives of those powers which had accepted the surrender of the respective enemy countries. For the purpose of participating in the drafting, France was considered as a signatory to the terms of surrender for Italy.
In all international agreements, as in all agreements, someone, at some stage, has to .set in motion the process of putting words on paper to represent the agreement; the work of drafting has to be begun somewhere. In this case it was begun by the council of [DOT]foreign ministers of the powers I have mentioned. They met at London for the first time on September 11, 1945 and a series of meetings were held which terminated on "October 2. The first draft of the Italian treaty was prepared by the representative of the United Kingdom, and it was tabled at this meeting; but little progress was made at the meeting because of failure to reach agreement on the procedure to be followed. This diffi-
(Mr. Claxton.l
culty was overcome when the foreign ministers of the United Kingdom, the United States and the Soviet union met at Moscow between the 10th and the 24th December, 1945. At thht conference it was agreed that the terms of the peace treaty with Italy should be drafted by the foreign ministers of the powers I have mentioned, and that the deputies of the ministers should immediately set about the work of drafting. It was agreed that they would resume their work in London. It was also decided that when the drafts had been completed the council of foreign ministers would convene a conference of specified members of the united nations which had actively waged war with substantial military forces against European enemy states, for the purpose of considering the draft treaties. Following this, those of the great powers signatory to the respective armistice terms would draw up the final -text of the treaties which would come into force immediately after ratification by the big four.
From January to April, 1946, the deputies of the foreign ministers worked in London on the preparation of t)he five draft treaties. A special commission was sent out to study the problem of the frontier between Italy and Yugoslavia. On April 25, the council of foreign ministers met in Paris to resume negotiations on the five peace treaties. At the first meeting it was agreed that France should participate in the discussions of all the treaties and not merely of that with Italy. From May 16 to June 15 the council of ministers met. They agreed on settlement of the Soviet claim to Italian reparations, the amount being fixed at $100,000,000, and on the principle of creating the free territory of Trieste. The French proposal, known as the French line, was accepted in regard to the Italian-Yugoslav frontier. On July 5, the council of foreign ministers issued an invitation to the other sixteen nations to attend the conference at Paris. The conference began on July 29 and met continuously until October 15.
In convening the conference, the council of foreign ministers had agreed between themselves to support the clauses in the draft treaties on which they had already reached agreement. The rules of procedure drawn up by the council and put before the conference for its consideration provided for recommendations for changes in the draft treaties being made by the conference by a two-thirds majority. At the very outset, this proposal with regard to the necessity for a two-thirds majority to make a recommendation resulted in a debate which at times became heated and undoubtedly adversely

Treaties oj Peace
affected the atmosphere of the conference. The view taken by the Canadian delegation as put forward by the Prime Minister was that we would not take an active part in the discussion of these rules of procedure. It seemed to us that we should get on with the work of the conference. The point was put time and again that in order to arrive at a treaty of peace it was necessary to have agreement. Peace could not be made by either votes or vetoes.
On a number of points of major importance the big four had not been able to reach agreement prior to the conference. Consequently on these points there was very active debate at all stages of the conference between representatives of the big four as well as all the other members of the conference. Some three hundred recommendations for changes in the peace treaties were put forward by representatives of the twenty-one nations. Those were considered in various commissions, and then the reports of the commissions were considered in the conference as a whole. In the final plenary sessions there were no less than 243 votes on these recommendations, which resulted in sixty recommendations for changes in the drafts being carried/ by a two-thirds majority and fifty-two by a simple majority.
Following the adjournment of the conference on October 15, the council of foreign ministers met at New York to draft the final texts. In their discussions they gave weight to the recommendations carried by a two-thirde majority, and the substance of a good number of these recommendations was incorporated into the final treaties. The treaties themselves have been signed by all twenty-one nations and by the five enemy states. So far as is known, none of the allied states or the ex-enemy states concerned have to date deposited ratifications, although in the United Kingdom a bill has been adopted to provide for approval of the treaties. It is believed that a number of the countries are ready with the constitutional steps necessary to effect ratification. The Paris conference was useful in that it gave all representatives of the twenty-one nations an opportunity to make themselves heard, to have the points debated, to secure information, and then to state where they stood in respect of all the points in issue. I believe this was an innovation in the methods of making peace; and in so far as it gave all the participating nations a voice, it was an improvement on previous peace-making procedure. Further, when the discussion had ended and the votes had been taken, the council of foreign ministers meeting at New York was able to reach agreement on every point that was in issue. Compromises were
worked out and for the most part the recommendations made at Paris were given effect to by the council of foreign ministers. %hereas before the Paris conference there were a great number of important points in respect of which the council of foreign ministers had been unable to secure agreement, following the discussions and expressions of opinion at the conference they were able within the next two months to arrive at agreement and to complete drafts of the treaties which are now before the house. So that it is quite impossible to say that the Paris conference did not accomplish anything. In the first place it was an improvement on treaty-making procedure, in this very important respect, that it gave the nations taking part in the war a chance to make their voices heard. In the second place it gave them a chance to indicate where they stood. In the third place it gave all five exenemy countries an opportunity to make their representations before the conference and before all its commissions. Similarly, opportunities were given to other interested nations. In that sense the conference was a democratic organ, proceeding, as far as the recommendations were concerned, on the basis of debate, discussion and vote following the debate.
The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) referred to a straw vote taken by some journalists. I think the number of journalist votes he gave would total some 120. Nobody knows how many journalists were at the conference, but the best estimate I heard was two thousand. So that 120 represent a fairly small proportion of the two thousand journalists who were attending the conference.

They may have. They may not have had the opportunity. There may have been some principle of selection. We do not know. But one journalist, who had great experience in these matters, when he asked if he regarded the conference as a success, stated that it was a success but it was a bad success- a succes triste. That represented a wide measure of opinion. The reason for that qualification was that at the conference there was brought out more sharply than ever before existence of a conflict of view between on the one hand the Soviet union and the five states which usually voted with it in such matters, and on the other practically every other nation represented there. The cleavages between these two were brought forcibly into the open, to indicate not only to the conference but to the people of the world the difficulties and the awful dangers implicit in this kind of cleavage
Treaties of Peace

through the whole machinery of international cooperation.
Hon. members may appreciate something of the size of the task of a conference of this kind when I mention it was estimated that in attendance at the conference there were some six thousand people, of whom about two thousand were delegates and their advisers, secretaries, messengers and so on; about two thousand were journalists, radio reporters, cameramen and the like, and about two thousand were members of the secretariat, almost entirely supplied by the government of France. The conference met at the Luxemburg palace, in the senate chamber, and proceeded speedily to hear speeches of a general character from the representatives of all the nations present, and then to deal with questions of procedure in a committee on procedure. When that committee reported back to the plenary conference its report was adopted after a number of votes and considerable debate. Ten commissions were created. One of them was the general commission which was to have been the steering commission, but it never met. The nine active commissions were the five territorial commissions dealing with the treaties with each country; the economic commission on the treaty with Italy; the economic commission on the treaty with the other Balkan countries; the military commission, and the legal and drafting commission, of which I had the honour of being president. The commissions met over a long period. Generally speaking they met every day from ten in the morning until one-thirty, from three-thirty until seven or eight in the evening, and frequently again from nine o'clock on. One commission met continuously from nine o'clock one evening until six-thirty the following morning, but that record was speedily beaten by the economic commission on the treaty of peace with Italy which met continuously, without interruption or adjournment, for a period of twenty-eight and a half hours.
The business of peace making, as I think hon. members will recognize from reading the records of the previous Paris conference, in 1919, or any other peace conference, is exceedingly arduous, requiring long hours and the hard work of large numbers of people. The Canadian delegation was not one of the largest by any manner of means. Where I think the Yugoslav delegation had a membership totalling something like three hundred, the Canadian delegation never totalled more than approximately thirty. Of all those present I believe the Canadian delegation was the most bilingual of all the delegations present at the conference. When the active work of
IMr. Claxton.3
the conference was well under wav, and for a very considerable period of the conference, every member of the Canadian delegation could understand and make himself understood in both French and English. The delegation also was fortunate in having as one, of its leading members our ambassador to Moscow, who speaks and understands Russian. As leader of the delegation at the end I should like to say how great a privilege it was to serve with such a devoted group of people, and I want to express thanks here, as I have done privately to them, for their very loyal work for Canada throughout the whole period. I do not believe any national delegation was better served by its advisers and members than was the Canadian delegation; nor do I think any of them worked harder or did more to try and ensure that the treaties of peace when finally drafted would be as good as they could be.
The conference had one unusual feature, in that instead of the steering being done by the general committee or a steering committee consisting of representatives of the conference, it was done by what was called the secretariat, which consisted of eight members meeting under the chairmanship of the secretary general. This was a new device at international conferences, and in the view of most delegations I believe it was one which should not be followed at future conferences if it can be avoided, because it departs from the principle of democratic control of the conference being effected by members of the conference as a whole. While this secretariat, as it was called, dealt largely with matters of procedure, sometimes those matters did affect the work of the conference in major particulars.
The hon. member for Peel said he did not think we followed the line we should have followed and I believe that remark was tied in with his following sentence, relating to the composition of the Canadian delegation not being represented by members of the various groups in parliament. That was a matter to be decided by the government, and in view of the fact that under our system it had to take responsibility before this house and before the country for what was done the government felt that course should be followed in connection with the execution of a treaty of this kind. The hon. member also suggested that the Canadian delegation should have raised a greater and more powerful voice at Paris. I suppose there is always room for remarks of that kind, but it would be interesting to know in what particulars the Canadian delegation erred. I would be very glad to go over with my hon. friend the 253 votes at the final session of the conference and the

Treaties oj Peace
thousands of votes of which we have record in the commissions, to see in what respect the Canadian delegation should have voted differently or spoken differently. I believe the line laid down by our Prime Minister for the conduct of the Canadian delegation, in his opening speech at the conference and in his oral instructions to the delegation, was one which met with the widespread approval of the Canadian people. At Paris it proved to be a sensible, reasonable and constructive line, and I think most of the delegations there recognized that the part played by our delegation had been helpful throughout and was designed, as the Prime Minister intended it to be and as Canadians would like it to be, to do everything possible to bring about the greatest possible measure of agreement on the best possible peace terms at the earliest possible date.
Our experience at Paris leads me to make some further remarks of a more general character. In the first place the Paris conference threw emphasis on the fact that we now have diplomacy by conference as a major agency of international cooperation. The vital importance of the matters discussed has increasingly resulted in negotiations being handled and decisions made by top-level spokesmen of each country meeting face to face at conferences, rather than to follow the older method of using- our diplomatic representatives in foreign countries. This has been brought about partly because of the greatly increased complexity, importance and interdependence of the questions which have to be discussed; and it results in part from more rapid means of communication and transportation.
The development however has placed a heavy burden on countries like Canada which have not had a large Department of External Affairs. The fact that, as the Prime Minister said, we had to attend some ninety-eight conferences in 1946 indicates the heavy load which must be carried by members of the government, and by the officials, advisers and staffs of the Department of External Affairs, and other departments concerned. Certainly my experience, having attended three major conferences in 1946, as well as attending to the other business with which I was entrusted, led me to believe that these conferences and this method of doing business expose people in public life to a continuous burden of overwork and overstrain which I do not think has been known before. But we cannot escape from this burden. The suggestion sometimes made in the house and elsewhere that we could stop going to conferences cannot be seriously regarded. Canada has worldwide interests. That has been shown
by her participation in two wars, and the fact that we suffered from the worldwide depression. We cannot escape from our responsibilities, and should also be ready to take advantage of our opportunities to make any contribution we can to international cooperation.
Having attended a great number of these conferences, and having seen the work that is done, my belief is that hon. members would be astonished if they knew the actual amount of drafting of international instruments done by our representatives, an amount out of all proportion either to the size of the country or the size of our delegations.
Another point which the Paris conference threw into greater prominence was the emergence of two or three super-great powers as a dominant fact of international cooperation affecting peace and security to a greater degree than any similar development has ever before affected peace, security and the opportunities for a good life.
In the third place the Paris conference likewise threw into sharper contrast than ever before the consistently opposing views of the east and west, of the Slav countries and the rest of the world. I have already referred to that, and it is evident to hon. members.
Further anyone who has been exposed to the necessity of conducting international affairs in the kind of atmosphere developed by these conferences must be conscious of the need for new techniques of international cooperation. It becomes increasingly important when there are differences of opinion, and when there are wide differences of ideologies and language, that nations taking part at international conferences, as well as the conferences themselves, should be particularly correct in -all their procedure, and that the rules of procedure should be worked out with much greater care than seems to have been done in respect of international conferences in the past.
Our experience at Paris was that the rules under which we worked could have been improved greatly. I ventured to bring this point out in my final speech at the closing plenary session. It was the only suggestion of its kind that was made; but I am glad to say that speaking privately many of the representatives at Paris agreed with this suggestion and felt that procedure had become of the utmost importance in arriving at workable machinery on which to find agreement
Our experience at the Paris conference was that its success and work was affected to a considerable extent by the discussions at the
Treaties oj Peace

start with respect to procedure, which might have been obviated haxi draft rules of procedure been circulated in advance to the nations coming to the conference, so that they could exchange their views, and then in camera before the conference began, arrive at common agreement with respect to the rules of procedure.
There was another feature at Paris which led to a good deal of discussion among the delegates, and that was as to how far peace negotiations could go when everything was done in public. The Paris conference, I believe, was the first major international conference that which not only plenary sessions but also the meetings of all the commissions were held in public. As hon. members will appreciate, this resulted in a number of speeches being made, not for the purpose of reaching agreement but for home consumption, for the purpose of dealing with one section or another of public opinion throughout the world. The view generally held by most delegations at the conference was that plenary sessions should be held in public, meetings of commissions, and certainly of subcommissions, should be held in private so as to facilitate the close discussion on points of drafting and the like.
These suggestions were discussed with the representatives of numerous delegations at Paris. I believe they met with a wide measure of support, and our hope is that if and when there are future conferences of this kind, they will be considered.
As I said, the peace conferences now before the house have resulted from some eighteen months of work. I am sure every nation worked for months before that on the preparation of their documents, maps and books of instruction, and our belief is that they represent the highest possible measure of agreement.
The hon. member for Peel has spoken about a desire that Italy should not be put into an economic straitjacket; our view was that everything possible should be done to enable Italy to take her place among the nations of the world so that she could become a contributor to the world's prosperity, and not a consumer of assistance from other nations. That was the view taken by the Canadian delegation throughout the conference. I might establish that by reading to the house a passage from a s/hort speech delivered by Mr. L. D. Wilgress, our representative on the economic commission for Italy, which he delivered before that commission on September 2, 1946:
The Soviet delegate made the point earlier in our discussions that the reparations provisions of the peace treaty will provide for Italian factories and Italian workmen. With this object 
we are in full agreement. But it is precisely to help Italy to provide work for Italian factories and Italian workmen that we wish to see Italy recover as rapidly as possible her export trade with as many foreign markets as possible. This will provide the means whereby the raw materials essential to the Italian economy can be obtained. The need for raw materials has not been overlooked and is covered by the provisions set forth in paragraph 4 of article 64. But, it is desirable that the economy of Italy should not be made too much dependent upon her commercial relations with any one country. This would run counter to the fourth principle of the Atlantic charter to which I have already referred and to which most of the countries represented here subscribed in the united nations declaration of January .1, 1942. By this fourth principle, the united nations committed themselves "to further the enjoyment by all states, great or small, victor or vanquished, of access, on equal terms, to the trade and to the raw materials of the world which are needed for their economic prosperity."
That was the view taken by the Canadian delegation, and that was the view put forward by other like-minded nations.

Treaties of Peace

The first few lines on page 4 of the treaty with Italy seem to indicate that the united nations wish to treat Italy very fairly, but I feel that the terms of this treaty with Italy are unjust in some particulars. That is only my personal opinion, but on reading the terms of the treaty I feel that if we had had a chance to study this in committee, if the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) had been a witness there, he might have been able to change my views.
The way I figure it out is that the conditions of this treaty are such that Italy will not be able to expand her own resources and carry out in a business way as which perhaps she would like to do. This treaty cuts into the frontiers of Italy; it deals with customs, railways, the control of water power and many other things. In trying to carry out the terms of this treaty I feel that the united nations should, and I am quite sure they will, treat Italy with all fairness.
While Italy was our enemy during the first years of the war, later she saw the light and to some, extent helped to turn the tide in the favour of the allies. We have thousands of people in Canada of Italian parentage. Those whom I know are good citizens. They own thousands and thousands of dollars' worth of property, and without doubt are helping to make Canada a better nation. Steps should be taken to see to it that these terms are carried out as fairly as possible.
In. future hon. members should have a chance to discuss treaties in the committee on
external affairs before they are brought to the house, or even after they are presented in the form of a resolution. I feel that Italy should be given every possible encouragement by Canada to rebuild what she lost during the last few years of the war, and I hope the united nations will see that she has that opportunity.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River):	Mr. Speaker, I want to say just a word, more particularly with reference to the treaty with Hungary. I do not wish to repeat tihe things that have been said already by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) and others, with much of which I agree. It is somewhat regrettable to me that in the efforts to build peace treaties with these countries it was found necessary to agree to the transfer of territory, for no other reason perhaps than to give to the receiving country what is known as a strategic frontier. I am afraid that the Paris conference must have agreed to some of these transfers, more as a means of appeasement of Russia than anything else. I can quite understand the difficulties they faced in drafting these treaties and coming to an agreement with countries having such widely varied approaches. Perhaps it would have been necessary, had we taken a very strong stand, to fight Russia now; but whether that was so or not I am afraid that in agreeing to the transfer of territory we have sown the seeds for future war and given occasion for bitterness in the minds of people which over the years may cause a deterioration in relationships so that war will become inevitable. May we hope, nay, may we fervently pray, that that will not be the case. I refer more particularly, Mr. Speaker, to the Hungarian treaty. I notice that three villages on the south Shore of the Danube, together with their cadastral territory-which I understand to mean units of agricultural lands around the villages that are set up as units for taxation purposes; I am not going to attempt to pronounce the names-were ceded by the treaty to Czechoslovakia. I understand that the reason given by those who claimed that the territory should Czechoslovakia was that it would be a strategical frontier rectification. We heard much of that during the time of the peace conference. The Czechoslovakians protested vigorously that they were peaceful minded; that they had always been so. In the light, of that, Mr. Speaker, it is difficult for ms to understand why they needed a strategic frontier. If they did need it, and if they were able to show during the time of the conference that they were entitled to it, I wonder why it was that they were not asked

to cede back to Hungary territories that were taken from -that country by the treaty of Trianon in 1920? So far as I can find out, no attempt was made to have Czechoslovakia cede back that territory which was taken away from Hungary by the treaty of Trianon. For over a thousand years Slovakia was a part of Hungary. During the time of the deliberations at the conference we heard a great deal of the mistreatment of the Slovaks by the Hungarians during that period. I seriously doubt whether these claims were well founded.
It is a matter of history that the Slovaks during the whole period were allowed to continue the use of their own language. It is a matter of history, too, that the Hungarians never molested the Slovaks in any way. They were allowed to live their own lives without molestation. If in spite of the treatment which the Slovaks had received at the hands of the Hungarians, they want to break away, of course that is all right; I suppose we have to wish them good luck, but it does seem to me that if they want to break away from Hungary now they should not be allowed to take a fairly sizeable piece of territory with them, particularly a piece of territory in which substantial groups of pure Hungarians have been rooted for centuries and in which they and their families have carried on agricultural pursuits in peace. By this treaty a slice of territory, where these Hungarians have lived in compact units, is to be taken away. The Hungarians, I understand, who have been there for so long, are being uprooted from their ancestral homes and are being sent to Sudetenland, particularly to work in the industries which have been established in that country. These Hungarians have always been agriculturists, not industrialists. They will not be happy under the new arrangements. Surely the conference should have had in mind the happiness of these people and their ancestral rights.
I have a good many Hungarian friends in this country, but not in my present constituency. I do not think there are many in Pe%?e River, but I represented many Hungarian people in the Alberta legislature for quite a number of years, and I got to know them, their history and their problems. I have been told by eye witnesses who have been in the old country within recent months that in parts of the territory which according to this treaty are to be ceded to Czechoslovakia, changes are taking place so that the idea can be spread abroad that they were not always Hungarian. The Czechoslovak authorities are demolishing and defacing gravestones that h ive been there for hundreds of years in an

effort to bolster their claim that the territory was not always pure Hungarian. Keeping in mind, Mr. Speaker, the fact that the Hungarians are neither Germanic nor Slavic, but a distinct race, this becomes a very serious matter. It is a serious thing to deface the evidences; the people in a given area have lived there for hundreds of years.
I claim that one of the important principles to be observed- in the making of peace treaties is that no country should be impoverished by transfer of territory so that it is in danger of losing its identity; that no transfer of territory should be allowed which would be a cause for festering sores in the minds of the people for many years,, which festering sores will eventually break out and lead to another war. In agreeing to the cession of these territories to Slovakia, apparently for strategic purposes, we are contributing to the impoverishment of a country which could for many years to come be a source of important trade to the trading nations. I hope we are not lending our hand to an unwise transfer of territory which will result in the impoverishment of Hungary.
There is one further matter. Hungarians, as a distinct race, neither Germanic nor Slavic, have always been a good balancing unit in Europe and we should insist that conditions be laid down so they might continue to be a balancing unit. On the other hand the Czechoslovaks, to whom the territory is being ceded, will always side with Russia because they are Slavic people. That, it seems to me, is a serious thing in the treaty with Hungary. I am disappointed at the transfer of territory provision, and I hope that when the minister replies he may have some information to give that will show that it just could not be avoided. I suggest that we are not justified in agreeing to this transfer of territory unless it is absolutely necessary in the interests of peace to do so. That is all I shall say at this time.

Then I will put these questions at the end of my remarks. The chief point I wish to make is to refer to the dearth, during my short parliamentary experience, of any opportunity to discuss foreign affairs. One wants to be fair, and I imagine that between the wars there were very genuine difficulties, genuine political difficulties about the existence of which we are all aware, that made people on both sides of the house, I suppose, wish to avoid the subject. But I think it was lamentable because it meant that the Canadian people were left in a kind of irresponsibility to some extent. They did not know enough of what was going on, and perhaps that was one reason why the people who did try earnestly to arouse public opinion met with the reception which was given them. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) was one of those who tried to arouse public opinion through the medium of the league of nations society, and who failed lamentably. We can remember the names of some of them-Sir Robert Borden, Hon. N. W. Rowell, Sir Robert Falconer, Sir George Foster.	Did those gentlemen get
thanks or admiration for their efforts? No. On the whole, they were laughed at. People said "We are only fighting animals, and we must fight again." Well, we did fight again.
The reason I suggest very earnestly that we should have debates in this country on foreign affairs, and debates that amount to something, is that in my view public opinion needs to be constantly stirred up. It ought not to be necessary, but it does need to be stirred up, and it should be stirred up so that we shall have ever present to our minds the formidable, indeed the devastating international problems which now face us. and so that we shall not slip into the attitude of mind, into which there is a danger of our falling, of being on the one hand more or less forgetful, or on the other hand, and that is just as bad, fatalistic and acquiescent.
I want to add a word as to the history, in my short parliamentary experience, of debates in tills house on foreign affairs, which debates I take it would naturally come when the estimates of the Secretary of State for External Affairs are before the committee. That is my understanding. I remember very well my first session in the House of Commons. We had been expecting the foreign affairs estimates, but they did not come until the second last day of the session, a day which I remember quite well because it was the Prime Minister's birthday. We joined in a dinner in the House
of Commons-Dutch treat-at which we did honour to the Prime Minister, and when we came down here into the chamber, to our great surprise we found him ready with his foreign affairs estimates. I had often been told of the Prime Minister's skill in timing, and that was an excellent instance of timing, because you cannot really go after a man in anything like hostile fashion after you have been at a dinner in his honour, and a very pleasant dinner it was too.
In the second session it was even worse.
I remember quite well, as I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs will remember, the 31st day of August last. It was the last day of the session, and there was in the house a remnant of members who had not yet gone home to pursue their businesses or their pleasures. It came to Saturday, August 31, and the estimates for the Department of External Affairs were brought down that day. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, kindly but persuasively and firmly, pointed out to us that unless we wanted to stay over for several days more, which no one very much wanted to do at that time, we should have to shorten the debate drastically, and of course it was shortened drastically. If I remember rightly, the hon. member for Peel, who has devoted a great deal of time and thought to these matters, was barely able to get half an hour in which to express his views. There were others who felt themselves in similar difficulties. Now, at this session, we are approaching the end of our labours, and it looks to me very much as though we might be in the same position again. I would therefore appeal to the Prime Minister and to the Secretary of State for External Affairs to see to it that the same thing shall not happen again.
In my opinion it is one of the duties of parliament to try to keep these affairs before the public so as to have them understood. I realize that governments have to govern; I realize that steps have to be taken to that end. I realize that they cannot debate everything they are going to do in parliament. I know all that, and I wish to take a common sense view of it. At the same time, however, I suggest that there ought to be time to discuss the principles that underlie the actions which governments have to take, so that when action has to be taken it is not something which parliament has never had a chance to consider, and we are not left with a situation such as exists now, perhaps without anyone intending it, in which parliament is treated like a lot of little children playing in the sand. We really have no right except to come and be told what has been done. We have never,

Having said that, I should like to ask two questions. One of them comes under article XXIII of the treaty with Finland. Under that article it is stated that the Soviet union is abating a very considerable amount of its claim for reparations against Finland and is settling on the sum of $300 million. It would be of interest, if the figure were available, to indicate how much of a concession that is supposed to represent. Another question I wish to ask has reference to article XXX, section 1, subsection 1, which speaks of Finland's giving the unconditional most-favoured-nation treaty to all members of the united nations. Subsection 2 qualifies that to some extent, and I imagine reasonably, by declaring that these undertakings by Finland shall be understood to be subject to the exceptions customarily included in commercial treaties concluded by Finland before the wrar. It would be interesting if we could be informed in a general way just what is the situation under that clause, and to what extent trade with Finland is being facilitated or is progressing. Those are two questions I should like to have answered.

My hon. friend may have his views; but I submit that, when you have gone through the process of peacemaking and arrived at the stage where the several nations involved have signed treaties, unless you are going to reverse everything which has been done or upset everything, which has been done and start all over again, the only choice left to you is to approve the treaties as they stand. From what has fallen from the lips of hon. members opposite, my hon. friend included, I should say there is not one member of this house who would wish to defeat the resolution approving these treaties. They may not like what is in the treaties. I myself was one of those who spoke most strongly against the way in which these treaties were brought into being. After Canada had taken the important part she had taken in the war for freedom. I protected that she had not been given a chance even to have a word with respect to these all-important treaties until they were placed before the conference in a more or less complete form by the council of foreign ministers, which was the body which had been agreed to by the great powers as the one which should take up the work of settlement at the outset. All of us in this house, I think, have already expressed ourselves very strongly; I think I might go so far as to say we have resented that these arrangements should have been made in the way they were. But I have always taken the view that if when the arrangements were made we had all known the circumstances under which they were made, perhaps none of us would have subsequently sought to alter the situation. No one will ever know what Mr. Churchill and President Roosevelt and others who were associated with them in some of the conferences had to consider as to what it was wisest to do at a particular moment. I am sure that some of the things they did, they did because of stern necessity and for no other reason; and some of the things which we have had to accept would never have been thought of for a moment and would have been resisted to the limit had it not been for the fact that everything considered, and with the war raging, what was done seemed to be the best course to be taken at the time.
Like the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, I have tried to act in a reasonable way. I have tried to look at this thing in a realistic light and ask myself the question whether it will serve any good purpose to try, at this particular time, to find fault with arrangements
which were made during the time of the war, and with regard to proceedings over which we had no control whatever. I will say that, if there was a possibility of anything being done by the external affairs committee which would cause this house to change its view in the slightest particular in regard to what is in this resolution, I would be quite prepared to say now that it is not too late, although we are near the end of the session, to refer these treaties to the committee. But I know there is not. I know' that all that might be discussed at the committee would not cause the committee to suggest one alteration in what is in the resolution before the house at the present time. In these circumstances I think it would be unwise to refer these particular treaties to the committee.
My hon. friend made one other point which I think has a good deal to it. He says that a discussion of these treaties would enable hon. members to learn a little more about the state of Europe at the present time and the difficulties which have developed since the treaties were signed, and might cause the house to consider with greater care whether later on these treaties should be ratified and the ratifications deposited. May I say to my hon. friend that I understand the committee on external affairs are to have a secret session in which they hope to discuss, and to get information upon, conditions in Europe at the present time which will give to the committee as full information as can be given by those who are informed in the Department of External Affairs. That information will be much fuller than could be given here, for the simple reason that there are some things in connection with the international situation at the present time which can be discussed privately, but which it would not serve the interests of the world at large to discuss publicly at the moment. With that opportunity made available, I think hon. members will be able to get such information at least as they would be searching for under this particular resolution, at least under reference of these particular treaties to a committee.
