Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the constitution of the international refugee organization, signed at Flushing Meadows, New York, on December 46, 1946, and that this house do approve the same.
He said: The house will be interested to know that nineteen states have now signed the constitution of the international refugee organization. Since I tabled the constitution in this house on April 30, the governments of

International Refugee Organization
Australia, Iceland, Belgium, Bolivia, the Argentine and Panama have signed the constitution in addition to the thirteen states which had signed prior to that date. Perhaps it might be well to place on record the list of those states who had signed at that time, in order to have the nineteen that have signed up to the present. The thirteen states which had signed prior to April 30 were: Canada, France, the United Kingdom, the United States, China, the Dominican Republic, Guatemala, Honduras, Liberia, the Netherlands, Norway, New Zealand and the Philippine Republic. Hon. members will remember that under the terms of the constitution it was not to come into effect until signed by fifteen states representing seventy-five per cent of the contributions allocated. The total contributions of these nineteen states to the operational budget would amount to 77-13 per cent. Therefore, if at least fifteen of these states whose total contributions are seventy-five per cent of the operational budget proceed to ratification, the constitution of the international refugee organization will, under the terms of article 18 thereof, enter into force. However, up to the present day only six of those nineteen states have deposited their instruments of ratification. They are the United Kingdom, New Zealand, Australia, China, Guatemala and Iceland, and the total assessment of these six states is only 19-51 per cent of the operational budget. But the United States is one of the governments which has signed the constitution; and the senate and house of representatives have voted in favour of a bill authorizing United States participation in the organization, which bill now only awaits the presidential signature. The United States contribution is 45-75 per cent, and that of Canada, 3-5 per cent, so I think there is every reason to expect that within a matter of days the minimum of fifteen ratifying states and seventy-five per cent of the operational budget will have been covered.
The preparatory commission of the international refugee organization is now meeting at Lausanne, and recently decided to undertake executive functions beginning tomorrow, July 1. In view of the end of UNRRA'S displaced persons' activities on June 30, it is essential that the IRO should be equipped to take over its work as soon as possible after July 1. The preparatory commission will have very limited funds and will be able to function only on a purely temporary basis pending the coming into force of the constitution of the organization. For this reason it seems to be of importance that ratification of the
constitution of the international refugee organization be effected as rapidly as possible.
The constitution itself has been fully discussed in the standing committee on external affairs, and I do not wish to take up the time of the house by referring again to the functions the organization is designed to perform. There are some points, however, it may be of some advantage to mention again at. this stage. The proposed budget of the international refugee organization is divided into two sections, administrative and operational. For the first financial year the provisional budget calls for the sum of 84,800,000, UR. funds, for the administrative expenses and $151,060,500.	U.S. funds, for	operational
expenses. Canada's assessment is 3-2 per cent of the administrative expenses, or $153,600, and 3-5 per cent, or $5,287,117, for operational expenses, a total of $5,440,717. Similar scales of contribution for the United States are, respectively, 38-89 per cent for administrative and 45-75 per cent for operational expenses. For the United Kingdom they are 11-48 per cent for administrative and 14-75 per cent for operational. The total United States contribution thus would amount to approximately $70,000,000, as against the figure of $5,440,000 for Canada. In addition to the assessment for administrative and operational expenses of the IRO, there is provision in its constitution for the raising of a sum of $5,000,000 by voluntary contributions from member states for expenses incurred in connection with schemes which may be undertaken by it for the large scale resettlement of refugees, as distinct from their resettlement as individuals or as family units. As contributions to this fund of $5 million will be on a voluntary basis, there is, of course, no scale of contributions. Mr. Jean Desy, Canadian ambassador to Brazil, has been acting as our representative at the meetings of the preparatory commission and has informed us that the next meeting of the full preparatory commission is scheduled to begin in Lausanne on July 15. At that meeting it is hoped that a sufficient number of ratifications to the constitution will have been received to make it possible for the organization itself to come into existence and to assume its executive functions.
In view of this, it would be encouragement to others to have it known as early as possible that Canada has ratified the constitution. For nearly eighteen months this problem of refugees has been fully discussed with the united nations. Canadian representatives have consistently taken the position that this great humanitarian problem can be dealt with only on a broad international basis. It is

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
International Refugee Organization
not only at the present time a serious hardship for those who are in the displaced persons camps but a serious burden to the occupying powers to provide for them and to maintain life in those camps.
I believe the people of this country wholeheartedly endorse the view that it is an international responsibility to which all of us should make some contribution. The constitution of the international refugee organization cannot be said to be a perfect document. It represents the efforts of fifty-five nations to find agreement -on a controversial political issue. Certainly there are clauses in the constitution which the Canadian government did not welcome and which our representatives unsuccessfully opposed in the committees and in the general assembly itself. Yet we have supported it because we believe it was the best compromise that could be achieved, and that if that one were not accepted and ratified there would not be any. If the united nations is to accomplish the job for which it was designed we, of course, have to recognize that the spirit of compromise is frequently called upon and forced to pretty extreme positions. But it was like the chanter of the united nations itself, that one had to be taken or we would not have had any at all. Thus the constitution of the international refugee organization, after long consideration, had to be accepted, or there would have been none. We felt that, as it was, it was a valuable international attempt to solve a problem which was an international responsibility. I hope, therefore, that the house will give its approval to the ratification of the constitution.
^ Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Peel):	Mr. Speaker, before the resolution carries, I should like to identify this party in support of it. This constitution has had the advantage of having been before the committee on external affairs. While it was before that committee, officials of the department expressed their opinions freely and generously with respect to such information as members of the committee required from time to time. For that reason I believe there need not be in the house any great division of opinion with respect to having this constitution approved as quickly a£ possible.
It is particularly important that Canada should not be hesitant in a humanitarian problem of this kind. Important foundations for our future policy were laid at San Francisco, the first recent international conference in which this country participated. I believe people in Canada aocept with some degree of pride the fact that in that portion of the charter of the united nations which deals with cultural and economic cooperation, per-(Mr. St. Laurent.]
haps more words were placed by Canadian delegates that by those of any other country in the world.

Yes, or several together. That is one of the features which would indicate the humanitarian trend taken by public opinion in Canada. It indicates, too, that Canada has been prepared in this field to place human values above property values, and to play its proper part in trying to do something for those needing help in other parts of the world.
In the constitution which has been placed in the hands of hon. members, I have noted with special interest the contributions therein set out. I believe 'the matter to which I shall now direct my attention, namely that of the percentage of contributions, was not discussed in the committee on external affairs, although similar discussion may have taken place in connection with it in another branch of the work of the department.
One point which will puzzle most Canadian people will arise in connection with these contributions. I am not for one moment suggesting that our contribution is too large, because I believe a suggestion of that kind would receive scant support. I believe, however, that there is at least a wide field for discussion of the contributions assessed against some of the so-called big powers.
The schedule showing administrative expenses shows that Canada would accept 3-20 per cent; France, 6 per cent; the United Kingdom, 11-8 per cent; the United States, 39-89 per cent and China, 6 per cent. Then I come to a big power which has a good deal to say and has made its mark across various countries of the world, sometimes very conspicuously.
I refer to the soviet socialist republics, which apparently desire to indicate that the communist way of life is a great and very successful way. But it would not appear that it is so successful, if one were to judge from these percentages. If my memory serves me correctly, the percentages set out in this schedule are along the same lines as those made to the general united nations organization by these nations. That being so, it would seem to me that there must be some significance in the fact that Russia is assessed only 6-3 per cent, or not quite double Canada's assessment with only 12,000,000 of population,
I am not one who wishes to raise unnecessary questions because, after all, there may be sound reasons why the budget is made up in this way. I am not for one moment suggesting that there is any criticism to be attached to Canada, to any of our delegates or

International Refugee Organization
to the government in connection with the present arrangement. I think, however, it does show one or two things. After all, as regards the system that has been held out to us so often as being a great system of government, if that is any indication of the success of that system with a country of 12.000,000 of population like Canada as opposed to a nation with a population of something like 150,000,000, when you take off some of the other republics, perhaps our system when it gets down to dollars and cents as a measure of success- and sometimes that is not to be disregarded as a measure-does show that this country has something to be thankful for. I believe that is an indication at least that some of the so-called big powers, when it comes down to making contributions to the united nations, do not compare too well with some of the so-called middle powers, including our own country. I only wanted to draw that to the attention of parliament and to the attention of the country at this particular time.
May I close my remarks with a word of caution. I have not the slightest criticism to offer at the moment in connection with this constitution, because I realize the urgency of the matter. It is now two years since Germany collapsed, and many people in these displaced persons camps have been leading a most unfortunate existence, an existence which only those who have seen their condition can appreciate. I should not like to see the united nations follow the practice which, I am afraid, too many nations are following, that of getting tied up too tightly in red tape. It may be difficult for Canada to say very much; all we can do is to raise our voice for reform in that regard.
I hope that this international refugee organization will not turn out to be just another nice looking organization on paper with a lot of fine speeches surrounding it and everybody getting worked up into great evangelistic fervour over the question of what is to be done for refugees and displaced persons. What must be done is for the nations to get together to try to solve this problem. Some nations will have to take more of these refugees than others. I do not think we can allow this constitution merely to stand without something being done, and being done in a hurry. I hope that this constitution with its many "ifs" and "whereases" will be better than some of the constitutions that have been passed.
That leads me to this one concluding remark. The united nations will have to take inventory in connection with these matters. The specialized agencies, of which this is one, are multiplying day by day. I have no doubt that many members of the government feel
as I do, that we must see that we do not overlap in connection with these various activities. Here we have an international refugee organization being set up. It is to be a brand new organization with all the powers and controls and legal language and the like usually found in such an organization. Only last week it was announced that we were to make a contribution toward a post-UNRRA programme. Then we have in Paris the meeting of the Big Four which are trying to arrange for the economic rehabilitation and reconstruction of Europe. Then there is the international trade organization which is meshed into all this.
The economic and social council was set up to coordinate the work of these various organizations, commissions and so on, but this task may be almost too much even for that council. The public must be getting confused because of the many organizations that are being set up within the united nations. We must do something in connection with that. Canada perhaps is in an awkward position; but some day, if my prophecy is correct, there will be a day of reckoning with respect to these huge organizations of the united nations. As I say, an inventory will have to be taken to see that we are not becoming top-heavy in our international relations.
This was brought up in the committee on external affairs, and last fall the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) made a spectacular speech before the united nations in New York when he brought up the question of the control and supervision over the expenditures by these bodies. That was an excellent idea, because a considerable amount of unanimity had been demonstrated in the external affairs committee in this regard, so much so that the motion for concurrence in the report was adopted by the whole house. I was glad to see that the minister expressed our views in New York on that occasion.
For some reason or another the international field is beginning to get like the domestic field in a lot of nations. We are just building up one thing on top of another, and every time we build up we are faced with another financial obligation for the country or the people in general. I only wanted to sound that note of warning; I was not speaking in criticism of this organization whose work must be carried out in a hurry. If there ate any faults in this constitution we shall have to let them go in the general belief that some action will be taken in connection with this matter in a practical way. But I just wanted these suggested reforms not to be lost sight of by the government or by parliament or by the people. As I say, there is

International Labour Organization
this top-heavy trend which, I am afraid, may interfere with the popularity of the united nations or might even undermine that organization which richly merits and deserves full support. That support may be forfeited if they do not keep within practical limits in connection with their constitutions, their general agencies and the organizations that are set up in the future.

That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the instrument adopted at Montreal on October 9, 1946, for the amendment of the constitution of the international labour organization, and that this house do approve the same.
He said:	Consequent on the dissolution of
the league of nations and the entry of the international labour organization into official relationship with the united nations, it became urgently necessary to amend the articles of its constitution relating to membership, financing and procedure for future amendments. Therefore an instrument for the amendment of the constitution was adopted at the 1945 (Paris) session of the international labour conference and was subsequently accepted by the necessary majority of the member states, becoming effective on September 26, 1946. Canada's ratification was authorized by order in council P.C. 2914 of July 12, 1946.
At the Montreal session of the international labour conference last fall, the new instrument of amendment now before us wras unanimously adopted and will come into force when ratified by two-thirds of the member countries including five of the eight members of chief industrial importance represented on the governing body of the ILO, of which Canada is one.
This instrument is designed to remodel the organization in the light of the experience gained in over a quarter of a century and to reequip it to discharge its responsibilities with greater efficiency.
The most important of the proposed amendments are designed to encourage wider implementing of the minimum labour standards embodied in conventions or suggested: in recommendations adopted at the various ses-

Inquiries of the Ministry
sions of the general conference of the member states of the organization. Canada, like other federal states, has been faced up to the present with constitutional difficulties in giving effect to the provisions of many of these proposals, which come within provincial jurisdiction. One of these amendments, article 19(7), is therefore of particular interest to Canada. It requires the federal government to arrange for periodic consultations between, the federal and provincial authorities with a view to promoting coordinated action to give effect to the provisions of such proposals. Another obligation is that fuller reports will be made to the international labour office as to the action taken or proposed to be taken by both the federal and the provincial governments on all these proposals.
Prior to the Montreal conference, the views of the provinces had been sought by the government on the proposed constitutional changes applying to federal states, and several of the provinces were represented at the conference by their ministers of labour or by their deputies.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: No, Mr. Chairman. I would say Canada is no more firmly ' committed than before the passing of this bill, because Canada has already undertaken that the united nations should have the immunities required to carry out the purposes for which the organization was formed. Less than an hour ago the house unanimously gave its approval to the international refugee organization, which in article 13 states:
The organization shall enjoy in the territory of each of its members such legal capacity as may be necessary for the exercise of its functions and the fulfilment of its objectives.
2. (a) The organization shall enjoy in the *territory of each of its members such privileges and immunities as may be necessary for the exercise of its functions and the fuffilment of its objectives.
This is a statute to provide that the governor in council may authorize the accession of Canada to the document which was drawn up, to set out in detail the immunity and privileges deemed to be necessary to permit the united nations and associated organs to carry out the purposes for which they have been formed. So it does not seem to me that we are com-
LThe Deputy Chairman.]
mitting Canada any more than Canada is committed at the present time. Article 105 of the charter of the united nations, to which Canada is committed, states:
1. The organization shall enjoy in the territory of each of its members such privileges and immunities as are necessary for the fulfilment of its purposes.
Paragraph 3 provides:
3. The general assembly may make recommendations with a view to determining the details of the applications of paragraphs ll and 2 of this article or may propose conventions to the members of the united nations for this purpose.
The general assembly proposed a convention, and that is the convention annexed to Bill No. 272. The purpose of the bill is to authorize Canada to accede to the convention. If Canada does so, with such reservations as are made, then we shall have a precise determination of what are the immunities and privileges regarded as necessary to enable the organization to fulfil its purpose. If we do not accede to the convention we still have the obligation in general terms, but we have not the details set out in the convention. Therefore I say we do not commit Canada any further. We dot the i's and cross the t's in the undertaking which we have already given, and which we gave again in connection with an associated organization this very afternoon when we approved the constitution of the international refugee organization.
Mr. DIEFENBAIvER: Personally I cannot see that the application of the united nations to Canada would be any greater by the adoption of this bill than has been the case heretofore. What it actually does, as I see it, is to carry into effect, into the world of the united nations, the immunities that ordinarily follow diplomats. If I read the history of diplomatic immunity correctly, however, the tendency in the last twenty years has been to restrict those immunities as far as possible. I did some reading on the matter, and found that the first general law on immunity, as far as Great Britain is concerned, goes back to the reign of Queen Anne. The Russian ambassador in England having been arrested, strong objection was taken by the Russian government, which resulted in the passing of the diplomatic privileges act of 1708, providing for diplomatic immunities which have been continued since that time. But on a reading of the Encyclopaedia of Social Sciences of 1932, one conclusion stands out. In view of the increasing number of the staff of the secretariats connected with the then league of nations, the tendency was to restrict diplomatic immunities in general as far as possible.

As I say, Canada has no intention of reneging on her international obligations. This country could not afford to do that. But I think my argument in an earlier debate today is supported. If we establish in this country immunities and privileges for a great number of people; if the average citizen of Canada sees that these people enjoy special rights in our courts and in other respects, they will say, and they will say it pretty quickly, "Why should I enjoy lesser privileges than the people who belong to another country?" When the committee rose we were giving some attention to the various widely ramifying branches of consideration into which this united nations subject might lead us through the passing of this bill to grant immunities. I think the hon. member for Peel gave the committee some sobering thoughts when he expressed the ideas I understood him to convey, that when the united nations organization was accepted at San Francisco in 1945 no one had the slightest idea how far it would branch out. Every member of this house who voted for the united nations organization in December, 1945, is, I believe, in the same position.
I believe it is the right of the Canadian people in the country generally who read Hansard to know something of the scope which this bill takes in. The newspapers are saying nothing about it; the radio is saying nothing about it, as far as I can make out; the people just do not know what is involved. I

should like to devote a few moments to the consideration of some of the things into which this bill can lead us with respect to men who have immunities similar to the one which the hon. member for Davenport referred to this afternoon. A man might be able to break the traffic rules with immunity and impunity.
In the first place, we are granting immunities to all the specialized agencies of the united nations organization. I think everyone will agree with that. The minister referred to several of these before he took his seat at six o'clock. May I list the ones he gave us on June 6 when discussing the matter. First of all, there was the international labour organization. Then there was FAO and UNESCO and the international "civil aviation organization, the international telecommunication union, the universal postal union and the world health organization. The minister was not quite sure whether he could accept the Bretton Woods proposals as coming under these united nations agencies.
I think it is fitting that we should give some attention to the possibility of Bretton Woods being one of these agencies. I do not wish to detain the committee, but there are matters concerning which the people have a right to be informed. The minister suggested on June 6 that the international trade organization would be one of the specialized agencies in all probability. Then there is the refugee organization to which we have just agreed today. There are probably others.
No one in the house, the minister least of all, would suggest that there might not be other specialized agencies. I might say, by the way, that the Bretton Woods agreements I regard as one of the most dangerous of these specialized agencies, and with regard to the Bretton Woods proposal, I think the members of the committee will be interested in a speech which was sent by President Roosevelt to the United States congress on February 12, 1945.

Then I will read this excerpt from President Roosevelt's message to congress in 1945, which indicated quite clearly the importance which he attached to Bretton Woods and his idea as to whether the united nations organization could function effectively at all without Bretton Woods. Before I read it, may I just draw this fact to the attention of hon. members and the people out in the country. When our representatives went to San Francisco they had the recommendations of two conferences to work upon. Those two conferences were the Dumbarton Oaks conference and the Bretton Woods conference. Of course, of those two, Bretton Woods constitutes one-half; so that
to suggest that Bretton Woods would not become a specialized agency of the united nations would perhaps indicate a little bit of carelessness in thinking. Having said that, may I read the statement which President Roosevelt made in his message to congress. It is as follows:
International political relations will be friendly and constructive, however, only if solutions are found to the difficult economic problems we face today. The corner-stone for international economic cooperation is the Bretton Woods proposals for an international monetary fund and an international bank for reconstruction and development.
I could refer to three or four other quotations from prominent United States statesmen of those days which, I believe,, would establish beyond any question that Bretton Woods is designed to become one of the specialized agencies. Hon. members and the people out in the country will recognize that this is a long list of specialized agencies, and some of these specialized agencies have wide ramifications of their own. Take UNESCO, for example. That is one of the most nebulous and most generally indefinite organizations before us today. Nobody knows what the scope of the activities of UNESCO ultimately will be, or what influence it will be able to wield upon the very children who are in their cradles and growing up today; who will set the programme which it is going to teach, and what control we shall have over that programme. There are, a great many other specialized agencies which are capable of development. Take the international trade organization. I almost tremble when I think of the possibility of that organization when it is fully developed, because of the things I know concerning the objectives of the men who are working to build up that trade organization, particularly people in the United States administration. There are all those specialized agencies. Just to indicate how wide is the interpretation of these immunities in regard to specialized agencies, may I read a little passage from the Canadian Bretton Woods Agreement Act of 1945? It may be argued that Bretton Woods is not yet one of the specialized agencies, but I will venture to say that it will be. So that this little quotation of a few lines has particular significance in this discussion. Hon. members will notice that in article IX, section 8, of the Bretton Woods Agreement Act passed in this house in 1945, the following words appear:
Immunities and privileges of officers and employees.
All governors, executive directors, alternates, officers and employees of the fund
United Nations

(i)	shall be immune from legal process with respect to acts performed by them in their official capacity except when the fund waives this immunity.
It may be said that is only "in their official capacity", but I will wager that it will be utterly impossible for anyone to demarcate exactly what will constitute acts in their official capacity. The section continues:
(ii)	not being local nationals, shall be granted the same immunities from immigration restrictions, alien registration requirements and national service obligations and the same facilities as regards exchange restrictions as are accorded by members to the representatives, officials, and employees of comparable rank of other members;
(iii)	shall be granted the same treatment in respect of travelling facilities as is accorded by members to representatives, officials and employees of comparable rank of other members.
I feel that I should say one thing with respect to what the minister urged a few minutes before six o'clock; and it was a wise and fitting remark which he made. He said that where any man today enjoying immunities commits an offence, representations are made to the nation which he represents and of course they deal with him. That is a thing which could be expected from a nation. But let us bear in mind that, in the case of these gentlemen, we are dealing, not with people who represent nations, but rather with the people who represent international organizations; and their bosses, shall we say, or their employers, will not be anywhere nearly so circumspect or punctilious about the disciplining of their officials and employees. Consequently we shall not have available to us the means which we now employ to bring the representatives of nations into conformity with our laws and practices.
So much for the specialized agencies. May I now turn for a minute or two to another class of people who are to be granted immunities under this act. A few minutes ago I referred to organs. May I now read from the united nations charter in respect of these organs. At page 76 of the booklet which I have in my hand, "Report on the United Nations Conference on International Organization," in chapter III of the charter, article 7, we read regarding organs:
There are established as the principal organs of the united nations: a general assembly, a security council, an economic and social council, a trusteeship council, an international court of justice, and a secretariat.
That is a rather large order. Clause 2 goes on:
Such subsidiary organs as may be found necessary may be established in accordance with the present charter.
There you have room for a very wide development beyond what we already have.

Surely this thing is a serious matter; it is far more serious than is the granting of immunities to the representatives of the nations of the world.
May I now turn to another aspect of the question, namely, the staffs. May I read again from the united nations charter, page 114 of the booklet on the charter that I have. Hon. members and the people out in the country will see another wide range of possibility. According to article 101:
1. The staff shall be appointed by the secretary general under regulations established by the general assembly;
Over which we have no control. Paragraph 2 of article 101 reads as follows:
Appropriate staffs shall be permanently assigned to the economic and social council, the trusteeship council, and, as required, to other organs of the united nations. These staffs shall form a part of the secretariat.
3. The paramount consideration in the employment of the staff and in the determination of the conditions of service shall be the necessity of securing the highest standards of efficiency, competence, and integrity. Due regard shall be paid to the importance of recruiting the staff on as wide a geographical basis as possible.
Inasmuch as the hon. member for Lake Centre raised the question of John Grierson this afternoon, I think it would be well for us to apply our thinking to this gentleman for a minute or two. Probably the reputation he has established is such that no one in Canada would be glad to know that this man was on one of the staffs or was on one of the special organs or one of the specialized] agencies, with freedom to come and go in Canada as he saw fit. Yet, according to the wording I have read, it is a distinct possibility that this gentleman would be so selected by the secretary-general, for example, over whom no nation has control. And I think it fitting that I should read something about that secretary-general, just briefly, to show what wide powers he has and what powers he has for mischief in case he should choose to use them. It may be argued that he will not use his powers for mischief. It can be argued that a lion will not use its teeth and claws for damage, or that a serpent will not use its sting, but the wise person takes great precautions in such matters.

Well, sometimes serpents have power to squeeze people to death, like the giant pythons. May I read just this word concerning the secretary general, and I am now quoting from article 97 of chapter XV of the charter of the united nations:
The secretariat shall comprise a secretary general and such staff as the organization may

United Nations
require. The secretary general shall be appointed by the general assembly upon the recommendation of the security council. He shall be the chief administrative officer of the organization.
I should say a person would not be speaking extravagantly if he said the secretary general, if he happened to be the right man, could become the super-dictator of the world; and it would be simply impossible to do anything about the matter. Now I read article 98:
The secretary general shall act in that capacity in all meetings of the general assembly, of the security council, of the economic and social council, and of the trusteeship council, and shall perform such other functions as are entrusted to him by these organs. The secretary general shall make an annual report to the general assembly on the work of the organization.
Nothing very serious there, but I go on to the next article:
The secretary general may bring to the attention of the security council any matter which in his opinion may threaten the maintenance of international peace and security.
If I were free, if the Chairman would consider it in order, I could comment on those words in a way which I believe would make the ordinary person in this country seriously concerned. Now I quote article 100:
In the performance of their duties the secretary genera] and the staff shall not seek or receive instructions from any government or from any other authority external to the organization.
We feel happy about that, because we say no nation is going to control this secretary general.
They shall refrain from any action which might reflect on their position as international officials responsible only to the organization.
2. Each member of the united nations undertakes to respect the exclusively international character of the responsibilities of the secretary general and the staff and not to seek to influence them in the discharge of their responsibilities.
Already I think hon. members will have wondered this. Suppose some international organization such as communism, or certain other great international organizations which all hon. members can think of but which I shall not name on the floor of this house, gained access to this secretary general. Suppose they did the dictating or the advising of the staff in accordance with their desires, and enjoyed all the immunities which are to be granted to these gentlemen in this country. Why, Mr. Chairman, the situation is appalling. It almost reminds one of the coming of a flight of locusts. These people will be everywhere. There will be hordes of them. They will be in our restaurants; they will be in our trains; they will be in our post offices-

subtopic: ACCESSION OF CANADA TO CONVENTION ON PRIVILEGES AND IMMUNITIES
speechtext: They will be in our hair.

subtopic: ACCESSION OF CANADA TO CONVENTION ON PRIVILEGES AND IMMUNITIES
speechtext:
Yes, they will be in our hair. They will be in a position to listen to practically everything said in this country, a situation which will simply render freedom of speech almost an impossibility if the right people are in charge in the united nations organization. As I said the other day, the ordinary citizen of this nation will walk in fear and dread of the most hideous bureaucracy the mind of man has ever conceived; and this bill provides for the immunity of all these representatives so that they can perform at liberty, without fear of any kind of check this country could possibly exercise over them.
I think I have said enough on this matter at least to arouse anxiety. I would say, let us go forward with the greatest of circumspection. We can do harm the seriousness of which we may not dream. Just before six o'clock it was said by the minister that if we found these people were beginning to get out of hand-these were not the words he used- and were overstepping their bounds, we would have to do something about the matter. Well, Mr. Chairman, ordinarily if you want to kill a snake the best time to do so is when it is in the egg stage, not when it is fully grown. I dare venture to suggest that when this terrible bureaucracy which has been pictured in the passages I have read is once thoroughly fixed, with its tentacles in every single phase of our lives, economic, social, political and everything else, it will be a matter of impossibility for this house ever to pass a regulation in any way curtailing these gentlemen. No government would dare bring in such a regulation. We have seen that sort of thing already with respect to the united nations and Bretton Woods. All the government had to do was simply bring in those measures and the members of this house just fell like ten-pins. Let any ordinary member reflect on the attitude that was taken by members of this house, except for the Social Credit group, in the fall of 1945, when we were discussing the united nations organization and the Bretton Woods agreement. Would the members of the house tolerate any intelligent discussion of the matter at all? Not a word. Any question of the motives? Not a word. Would they permit me even to speak, as they are indulgently doing now? No, sir; there was a chorus going on; and hon. members who were here can remember that a whole body of men on the Liberal side were literally deriding every word I uttered. Why? Just because the members of the house had accepted this thing; because there had been a widespread, highly paid, skilfully worked up

United Nations

propaganda going on in this country for three solid years to condition the country into readiness to accept the united nations organization and all its works, whatever it meant; and the Bretton Woods agreement, whatever it meant.
Already hon. members have found that the united nations organization is a disappointment. As a means of preventing war, as far as we can see today, as we approach the possibility of another calamity, it has no power at all; bnt in these dreadful aspects of it, these secret, hidden things as hinted in this bill, it has 100 per cent strength. They are right here in this measure we are passing. They will go on developing, whether the united nations ever does any good in preventing war. That is a very serious matter.
Then I think I should spend just a moment or two on the Bretton Woods agreement; I believe I shall still be in order. Has that agreement done anything in the world to improve the economic conditions of the world up to the present time? Not a thing.

Old Age Pensions
security and tax reform will be given effect to and the wishes of the provinces which desire to have that programme established will be complied with.
In regard to the suggestion which has been made over and over again, that there is something wrong with provinces making a supplementary grant, I will only say this. subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY

In that case, taking th. best interpretation that can be put upon it, namely, that the 810 supplement will be allowed in addition to the S600 maximum income for single people and SI,080 for married people, I would point out to the committee just how this works out and why it is that I am very much against the means test and hope that at the earliest opportunity it can be abolished. As it stands now, if a person is

Old Age Pensions

allowed an outside income of $240, which, added to the $360 dominion pension, makes $600, an amount of $20.90 a year saved by the individual from the age of thirty until the age of seventy would accumulate a sum sufficient, under the government annuities branch, to produce the amount of $240.
I claim that $21 a year is not a large amount to save, and yet there is no incentive whatsoever for a single person to save beyond $21 a year unless he can save more than $50 a year, which would bring him into the brackets of over $600 a year through the purchase of an annuity with these annual savings; or in the case of a married couple, putting the best interpretation on the Ontario addition of $10 a month, .they are now allowed $360 of independent income beyond their dominion government pension, and to accumulate that amount of money between the ages of thirty and seventy would require an annual saving of $31.44 or, in round figures, $31. There is no use in saving beyond that amount a year unless they can save more than $94, $94 being sufficient to buy them an income of $1,080 if saved over a period of forty years.
So that you have that large area for a married couple, saving between $31 a year and $94 a year, which practically embraces about seventy-five or eighty-five per cent of our whole population, and there is no use in people saving beyond $31 a year unless they can save more than $94 a year. That to my mind, as I am sure it will appeal to the minds of all hon. members, is an extraordinary situation and one which should be rectified at the first opportunity. I saw nothing substantial in this bill which goes toward that rectification. When you have a means test such as we have had, old people who might be able to earn a reasonable amount of outside income by serving as handy men or watchmen or doing work of that kind, are prevented from engaging in these useful pursuits, because anything they earn merely reduces what they otherwise would have through government old age pension.
I suggest that great consideration be given to the point I have made, that it is inadvisable for married people to save beyond $31 a year unless they can save more than $94. That amount may not sound like a large sum to many members here; but when it is realized that the average citizen cannot purchase his own home, even a humble home, a saving of nearly $109 a year is a very substantial amount, because they find great difficulty in making ends meet without providing for their own old age, as I am sure the minister will

admit, since that is the sum and substance of the matter that is before us.
So that when we put. this halter on savings, this premium on thriftlessness, it works against all our people. I would point out to the minister that many companies throughout the country are today putting into force a company pension or retirement plan, and very few of them can hope to give their employees more than $1,080 a year, which is what the dominion pension, plus outside income of $360, would allow. In fact, if that pension amounts to $300 or $400 or $500 at the end of the working term it will be quite an achievement in view of what has gone on in the past and what has been possible.
I believe that if the government does not do something to eliminate, the means test, particularly in the lower brackets, it will work to the disadvantage of men who would otherwise receive some recognition from the companies for which they work. I would ask him to give the matter even fuller consideration than he has so far given, because I can imagine nothing that works against the principle of self-help, which we should encourage in our people, so much as the operation of the arrangements which are now being put on the statute books. I would ask the minister to do something about this at the earliest opportunity, if not tonight, because the further away he postpones the opportunity which should be given to people to provide for their own old age, the more trouble he is heaping up for himself in the years to come. If he would make it possible for people to become reasonably self-sufficient; if he would give them an incentive instead of taking it away from them, his labours in the future would be lightened. I hope the time will come before long when we shall have a compulsory contributory old age pension plan for our old people.

It seems to me that if the pension authorities wish to do any chiseling, they have a good opportunity there to keep stalling people off month after month. It is my suggestion that the pension should be retroactive from the date of application.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
compare the regulation I have just read with the old regulation, he will see that we have tried to meet that problem.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: That is where I think these people need more consideration. subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I wish to say a word on this section. I spoke the other day in regard to the making of regulations. The act is quite clear; and although the minister has said that when the regulations are made-and I think I am using his own words-the provinces along with the federal authorities make the regulations. That is not according to the act.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
That is an important point. I have stated the position often, and what I

have said is the case. Where does my hon. friend get the authority for the statement he has made? I can only repeat that the act is clear in the matter. We cannot do that. If my hon. friend does not believe that, all right; I cannot say anything stronger than what I have said. But that is clearly the case, and I think he knows me well enough to accept that.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I suggest to the minister that section 19 (i) should read in this fashion, "The governor in council, together with the provinces, may make regulations." If those words are added, it will definitely imply what the minister has said.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: No. Somebody has to pass the regulations. Then they have to become law. subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: If a majority of the eighteen representatives of the provinces met here in Ottawa and decided on a certain regulation or change in a regulation, if they then recommended that to the minister, is he bound to put it through? speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I cannot say any more than I have already said three times.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: But it is important that the minister answer.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I have answered it three times.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: No, you have not answered it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: There is the law, and it is as clear as daylight. I must be at fault.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
I think the members of the committee are entitled to an answer to that question. It is a simple question and the minister can answer it yes or no. Old Age Pensions
inces at that interprovincial board meeting here should be unanimous in their adoption of a regulation or their recommendation of a change in an existing regulation, would the minister say he would be bound even by that?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: No.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I just want to make one point clear, and to amplify what has been said by the previous speaker. The minister has indicated that there are. some agreements and some regulations still not complete?

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: None of the agreements has been completed.

speechtext: There will be further modifications?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: As soon as this bill becomes law we shall have to obtain agreements.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: The minister said it was expected that there would be further meetings with the provinces at which certain matters could be taken up. One question came into my mind in connection with the $2,000 of property value that might be left in the hands of the pensioner. Some of the provinces have been conceding that, and for some time they have been as lenient as possible in the administration of the regulations. As the previous speaker said, the provinces come here and they have cases in which the regulations are working an injustice. speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Go on.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: That is correct?

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Is that fair to the provinces, who are supplementing the pension, doing their best to give pensioners reasonable security? Is it fair to hold the provinces down to that extent?

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: It is not holding them down.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I do not understand what the hon. member for Lincoln means when he says that.

speechtext:
As the hon. member for Peace River said, eighteen representatives of the provinces come here and agree unanimously to a certain proposed change in the regulations. Are the provinces not allowed to
have any say in this matter, by agreement or otherwise, in order to make any change under the regulations, in view of the fact that they are paying increased sums to help bring more security to the people of their provinces? speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: No one said that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext: The regulations are a contract. They cannot be changed except by agreement between parties, and I cannot say more than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: It is a matter of cooperation and consent.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: If the regulations are shown to be working a hardship they cannot be changed without the consent of all the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I can only point out for the fifth time the implications of the section, which are pretty clear. subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: No, it is not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Then I cannot make it any clearer.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: No.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Nothing?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: No; we get along very well.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Then what was the reason for the minister saying he was going to take up certain matters?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I was referring to agreements under section 2 of the bill.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Then there are agreements still to be effected?
Old Age Pensions

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: When this bill is passed, the provinces will be called upon to pay more money, and the bill will likewise be imposing upon the dominion an additional financial obligation. subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: We should be clear, I think, as to what is meant by the agreement the minister is talking about, and my feeling is that there is some misunderstanding now. speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Yes; that is purely their own affair.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: All that is provided under this bill, then, is that, according to the regulations that have been made, with the provinces and the federal representatives sitting in, the government will pay a pension of $30 or whatever lesser amount a province may pay, subject to the provisions of sections 4 and 5 of this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: The questioning has become so popular I do not see why I should not get in on it also. Did I understand the minister to say that in order that the dominion might make a change in the agreement with New Brunswick, let us say, all the other provinces had to agree. Did I understand that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: No.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: All that is necessary is agreement between the dominion and New Brunswick?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
There was confusion
between the regulations and the agreements. An agreement is a matter between the province and the dominion under section 2 of the bill.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: That is what I thought. Then I misunderstood you, and perhaps some others misunderstood you also.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: This is a filibuster.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: My hon. friend should know a lot about filibusters; I have seen him in a few.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: The minister who made that side remark probably knows all about it. If he wants to make it appear that way I can assure him he will get plenty of it. I am trying to get information.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: No, it is not carried. The minister had an opportunity a minute ago to save a lot of time by answering the question asked by the hon. member for Peace River. He has not yet answered it. It could have been answered briefly.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY

speechtext: If he did his humble best, then I would advise him to try something better, because it could be answered yes or no. If that were done, would it be considered supplementary and, therefore, not deductible from pension? The minister replied that if it came within section 16-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY

speechtext: The hon. member has the wrong regulations.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
I have not the new ones. However I am correct in understanding that that would be a supplementary payment. But any money coming from any private source or from other than a government source would not be suppleme ltaiy and would, therefore, be deductible.

Old Age Pensions

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: If it is income, yes.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I have another question to ask. These regulations I have are dated 1944.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Let us discuss the new ones.

I will see if this is in the new ones. Yes, I find it is the new regulation 24 which, under the heading "Suspension of Pension," states:
The payment of a pension shall be suspended (a) during the absence of a pensioner from Canada; provided that the pension authority may continue the payment of pension for any period of absence not exceeding ninety days in any one year where, in the opinion of the pension authority, the circumstances warrant such payment.
That is a slight improvement over the old one. But I would ask this question: Why does there need to be any time limit on a pensioner's being in another country if that country is better for him, or if his health is better there? If he has earned, by having been a resident of Canada, the right to receive an old age pension from Canada, why should he be restricted as to his movements after that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I do not think we can possibly ask the people of Canada to pay money to people, let us say, living in the state of Colorado or California.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Can a judge leave Canada on his pension?

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: It becomes a matter of opinion. I do not see why the people of Canada-and I am one of them-should object once in a while to pay a pension because the pensioner who has attained a certain age in this country wishes to go to another country.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Does any other country do it?

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not believe that ever in any debate I compared Canada with any other country.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: You all do.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I never do.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: You do, with New Zealand, all the time.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: My hon. friend surely is not asking us to do something in that regard that no other country is doing. Surely he is not suggesting that.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I am not concerned with any other country.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: You all are over there.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: If we agree in Canada to pay somebody a pension because of certain qualifications he has gained here, then why should he not have that pension, no matter whether he goes to Oregon, Colorado, or up to the Yukon if he likes? Why is the old age pensioner singled out as having to stay in Canada when he is likely to be a citizen who probably needs a better climate than Canada can provide? What is wrong with being somewhere else?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: It is wrong for the reason that the present Prime Minister of New Zealand said the same suggestion was wrong, when the matter was discussed in the New Zealand legislature in 1938. My hon. friend is about to say that surely I am not going to rely upon the Prime Minister of New Zealand. I will rely upon any authority which meets my case.

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I rely upon authorities, too. I do not want the Prime Minister of New Zealand for it, however; I will take the Minister of National Health and Welfare for Canada, if he will give us a good reason for it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I do not think-

subtopic: INCKEASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY

I will have to be absurd,
then, because I can see no difference between old age pensioners and judges, when one gets much more than the other. And when they live on Canadian money, I can see nothing absurd when the suggestion is made that they should both be allowed to live in the same place.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext:
The bill will be distributed after first reading. The general purpose of this bill is to extend the scope and usefulness of the Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act. As all hon. members are aware, loans are available under the act to veterans, through the chartered banks, for a variety of purposes associated with the establishment or expansion of a business or profession. These loans are subject to a partial government guarantee on a pooling basis similar to the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the home improvement plan, amounting to twenty-five per cent of the first million dollars of loans made by any bank plus fifteen per cent of any amount above a million dollars. Veterans . loans are made directly by the banks, but it is necessary for the Department of Veterans Affairs to concur in applications to ensure that those who apply are bona fide veterans within the meaning of the act.
The Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act has now been in effect for about six months. During that time, namely from January 15 to June 17, 1947, the Department of Veterans Affairs has concurred in 2,271 applications for loans by veterans in an amount of 83,943,000. This is a very considerable volume of applications acceptable to the banks, and indicates, I believe, that the act is fulfilling in large measure the functions for which it was designed and enacted.
Unfortunately, even though the banks are willing to lend money under the act, the veteran sometimes finds that he is unable to proceed as rapidly as he might wish with his investment, because of difficulties in
!Mr. Abbott.!
obtaining the necessary equipment and supplies. Hence, for this and other reasons the figures of actual loans made, which incidentally are not yet available for the second quarter of lending operations, are tending to lag behind the figures relating to concurrence by the Department of Veterans Affairs which I have just given.
I laid on the table this afternoon the first report covering operations under the act, in which is given an analysis of lending operations to date.
As a result of experience under the act, three principal amendments are being proposed, all of Which will facilitate the making of loans.
The first is an amendment designed to permit loans to a veteran who is already in a partnership and who wishes to assist in expanding the partnership business. Under the act as it now stands, this is technically impossible, even though a veteran may obtain a loan to form a new partnership or to buy into an existing partnership.
The second amendment is to meet the case of a veteran Who could not wait for the act to come into force and decided to invest what capital he had in a business. This veteran now wishes to expand and finds that he is no longer in possession of the one-third cash which he is required to put up before obtaining a loan under the act. The proposed amendment will permit the bank to regard expenditures made by the veteran between September 1, 1946, and January 15, 1947, as part of his proposed total expenditure, and therefore enable him to dispense in whole or in part with the ordinary cash requirement.
The third amendment is designed to simplify the taking of security under the act on personal and movable property. Because of lack of authority to take such security in their own right, the banks, where required, have been taking such security on behalf of the crown to secure the government's guarantee. This is extremely cumbersome and tends to place difficulties in the way of lending. The proposed amendment enables the banks to take security in their own right on personal and movable property which is the subject of a loan under the act.
The remaining amendments are of a clerical nature.
